messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
In those lines, Majid/Majeed does not immediately read as the same “cunning and apathetic” figure from the larger narrative. The excerpt shows urgency and physical responsibility: he is carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin quilt, while Rahima follows bewildered, and the bright moonlight even blinds him. That detail does not suggest cold indifference; it suggests exposure, haste, and bodily care. So the line itself offers a partial counterpoint to his established cynicism or detachment.

At the same time, because his earlier characterization is cynical and calculating, the action is not easily read as pure deontological good-will. A deontological reading would mean he is acting from duty, moral obligation, or selfless concern: “I must save them because they are mine to protect.” But the line’s phrasing—“I am going to take both of you to the village”—also sounds strategic. The destination matters. Moving them to the village may be practical, safer, socially expected, or a way to restore control after danger. That makes a teleological reading strong: he acts because the outcome seems useful, necessary, or less risky.

So the most defensible reading is hybrid, but leaning teleological. The act has a trace of duty or protection, especially in the physical image of carrying Jamila, but it is not presented as an unselfish moral impulse. It is more consistent with a calculated response: move the vulnerable people to a place where the situation can be managed. Given Majid’s broader portrayal, this looks less like spontaneous benevolence and more like pragmatic action shaped by consequences.

Required palindromes: kayak radar level rotor refer madam rotator racecar repaper reviver
